analysis.one_liner: Phases out routine antibiotic use in farm animals to keep human antibiotics working.
analysis.headline: The bill had 51 House sponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug makers to prove that using certain antibiotics routinely in cattle, pigs, and poultry poses no risk of creating drug-resistant bacteria in people. If a maker could not show that within two years, the FDA would withdraw approval for that routine use. It would also ban giving these antibiotics to whole barns of healthy animals just to prevent disease, allowing treatment only when a specific disease was actually present or a real outbreak risk existed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics: anyone who could face a bacterial infection, surgery, chemotherapy, or childbirth. The bill's findings cite CDC estimates of 2 million antibiotic-resistant infections and 23,000 deaths a year, plus $20–$35 billion in added health care costs. Preserving antibiotic effectiveness protects patients and lowers those costs.

how_it_helps.text: Within two years, the FDA would have to withdraw approval of a medically important antibiotic's routine non-sickness uses in food animals unless the drug maker demonstrated a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance.

It would ban routine dosing of healthy animals through feed or water for growth promotion and blanket disease prevention, allowing drugs only for treating a documented sickness or a specific, demonstrated outbreak risk, in the smallest groups and shortest duration possible.

The bill's findings cite the CDC's estimate that resistant infections cause at least 2 million infections, 23,000 deaths, 8 million extra hospital days, and $20–$35 billion in excess annual health care costs, and note the EU banned growth-promotion uses in 2006 without reducing livestock output.
More than 400 organizations, including the American Medical Association and the Infectious Diseases Society of America, supported this kind of phaseout, according to the bill's findings.

analysis.who_pays: Livestock producers and animal-drug companies that rely on routine antibiotics to fatten animals cheaply and prevent disease in crowded conditions. Some of those costs could eventually show up in meat prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial livestock producers and animal-drug makers

drawbacks.text: Farmers would lose a tool for cheaply managing disease in large herds, and transition costs could raise meat prices for consumers in the short run; the bill's own findings acknowledge producers would need to change practices, as European producers did after their 2006 ban.

The two-year withdrawal deadline is aggressive, and withdrawing approvals quickly could constrain veterinarians' options for managing outbreaks on large operations, though the bill allows non-routine disease control when a specific disease is present on the premises.

Opponents of similar measures have argued the FDA's voluntary industry guidance could achieve reductions without a statutory mandate, which the bill's findings dispute by noting antibiotic sales for food animals rose 16% from 2009 to 2012 under the voluntary approach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a documented public health threat — bacteria that resist the antibiotics modern medicine depends on — and the European experience cited in the bill suggests farming can adapt without output losses. The real costs fall on producers who have built low-cost operations around routine antibiotic use, and some may reach consumers as higher meat prices. Whether that trade is worth it is a judgment call, but the bill's supporters included the nation's major medical societies, and the bill itself notes the FDA declined to act on its own 1977 finding that low-dose livestock feeding promotes resistance.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and no vote ever happened there or on the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Louise Slaughter, a microbiologist by training, introduced the bill on March 16, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the committee's Health Subcommittee, where it remained without a markup or vote.
The bill attracted 50 cosponsors, all Democrats.
After Slaughter died in March 2018, Rosa DeLauro took over as first sponsor in May 2018 by unanimous consent, but the bill still never advanced.
The Congress ended January 3, 2019, with the bill having received no committee vote and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Livestock producers and animal-drug makers kept the ability to sell and use routine antibiotics in feed, and the public kept bearing the cost of growing antibiotic resistance.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-controlled committee never scheduled action on it.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to dose healthy animals through feed for growth promotion and blanket disease prevention, a practice that cuts feed costs in crowded operations. Public health groups consider that practice a major driver of antibiotic-resistant infections in people, so the industry's interest in keeping it runs against the public's.

The FDA would have to withdraw approvals for non-sickness uses of medically important antibiotics unless makers proved no human-health risk, shrinking a large market — the bill cites 13.5 million kilograms of antibacterial drugs sold for food animals in 2010 versus 3.3 million for human use.

industries.industry: Human antibiotic manufacturers and public health system
industries.note: Preserving the effectiveness of existing antibiotics protects the value of current drugs and avoids the CDC-estimated $20–$35 billion a year in excess costs from resistant infections, benefits that flow to patients and the health system alike.
